source.title: MEGABYTE: Predicting Million-byte Sequences with Multiscale Transformers
source.authors: L. Yu; Daniel Simig; Colin Flaherty; Armen Aghajanyan; Luke Zettlemoyer; M. Lewis

record.tranche_reason: The study measures bits-per-byte across model-size and architectural-configuration variations, bearing on parameter/loss behavior and architectural sensitivity, but it does not fit or replicate the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: Table 10 reports loss for three compute- and data-matched MegaByte configurations with different global and local model sizes. Table 9 reports loss at three patch sizes and describes performance as similar across a wide range. Neither table fits a power law or tests token- or compute-scaling laws. The reported global-versus-local allocation is an internal MegaByte architecture choice, not the parameter-versus-token allocation in V3.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper. It uses Kaplan et al.'s FLOP approximations and compute/data matching as tools and reports its own model's bpb against baselines. No experiment varies parameters, tokens or compute to trace a loss curve. None fits or extrapolates a power law, finds a compute-optimal parameter/token split, or holds parameter count fixed while varying depth or width. Tables 9 and 10 hold compute fixed and vary MegaByte-specific hyperparameters (patch size, global/local split), which is a different construct from V1 or V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: MegaByte outperforms byte-level baselines across text, image and audio at matched compute, and is competitive with subword models. The authors note the experiments are far below state-of-the-art scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a multiscale architecture and its configurations; it does not fit the original scaling-law curves or reproduce their extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Image256 bpb varies slightly across the tested patch sizes; the authors report similar performance across a wide range.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched compute and data on Image256, patch sizes 48, 192 and 768 give similar bpb (3.178, 3.158, 3.186). The authors report similar robustness across modalities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss of multiscale byte-level transformers is insensitive to patch size over a wide range at fixed compute.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched compute on PG-19, shifting parameters from the local to the global model lowers bpb (1.014 to 1.002 to 0.991). The authors say a global-heavy split is optimal across modalities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In patch-based multiscale transformers, the compute-optimal allocation puts most parameters in the patch-level global model.

record.problems: The model-size experiment reports only three compute- and data-matched configurations, with global and local model sizes changing together; it does not fit a scaling curve. The patch-size comparison does not hold total parameter count fixed. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these results.

untested.parts: No loss-vs-parameters, tokens or compute curve; all comparisons are compute-matched.
No depth/width variation at fixed total parameter count.
Image and audio results are single compute-matched comparisons, not power-law fits.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and V1/V4 links over-read compute-matched architecture ablations as scaling evidence. The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only to motivate compute matching and to compute FLOPs.

versions.untested_parts: Only a limited set of PG-19 model configurations is reported; the study does not fit a power law, test several orders of magnitude, or test token- and compute-scaling.
The study does not test how loss-minimising parameter and token counts vary with compute.
The patch-size experiment is on Image256, and total parameter counts are not held fixed; the study does not broadly vary depth and width at a fixed total parameter count.
The image and audio experiments report task performance, not whether the same power-law form holds in those modalities or regimes.
The study does not examine fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curves departing from power laws.

rows.subject: MEGABYTE
rows.operation_detail: Compared PG-19 performance across compute- and data-matched configurations with different global/local model sizes.
rows.note: The study reports increasing global-model capacity as improving performance, but this point alone does not establish a power law.
rows.check: Compute-matched global/local split on PG-19 (Table 10). Total compute is fixed, so this is not scaling in parameters, tokens or compute (V1). Total parameters also differ across configs, so it is not V4.
